title: AI 420 · Module 1 · Lecture Part 1: Inference vs. an Agent

lines: Welcome to AI 420, Agentic AI. This is Module 1, Lecture Part 1: inference versus an agent.
In about three minutes, you'll see the one idea this whole course is built on.
Start with inference. That's one request, and one response.
The model answers from whatever it learned in training.
It can't look anything up, and it can't check its own work.
An agent puts the same model in a loop.
It can ask for an action. That's called a tool call.
It sees the result. That's called an observation.
Then it decides what to do next, until it decides it's done, or it runs out of steps.
Here's a question to try both ways.
How many years before the first iPhone was the Space Needle completed?
A single call often gets it right, from memory.
But sometimes it says 47, or mixes up the year the Needle opened with the year it was designed. And it sounds just as sure.
The agent looks up the Space Needle: 1962. Then the iPhone: 2007.
Then it calls the calculator: 45.
The interesting part isn't that the agent got it right.
It's that the single call's right answers and wrong answers look exactly the same.
The agent shows how it got there, so you can check every step.
Three common mistakes.
First: calling anything with a model in it an agent. A chatbot that answers in one call is inference. The loop is what makes an agent.
Second: treating a right answer as proof. Ask how the answer was reached.
Third: reaching for an agent first. Agents cost more calls, tokens and time. Many tasks are better as one call, or a fixed script.
Before you move on, a quick check.
Name one question a single call can answer reliably, and one it can't. Then say what the second one needs that the model doesn't have.
Next, in Part 2, you'll see the four components of an agent, in about sixty lines of code.
